newsitem.title: USA: New Yorkers still fear crime despite drop - poll.
newsitem.headline: New Yorkers still fear crime despite drop - poll.

text.p: Most New Yorkers fear becoming victims of a crime despite the official view that the city has become safer, according to a poll released on Wednesday.

The poll, which reflected the complex perceptions of crime in a city long notorious for violent misdeeds, also found that at least half the respondents felt New York City was safer than it was three years ago.

The survey by Quinnipiac College in Hamden, Connecticut, contacted 845 New York City residents who said they were registered voters. It was conducted on Feb. 3-9, and has a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points.
By a margin of 65 percent to 34 percent, New Yorkers said being a victim of a crime was something they personally worried about, according to the poll.
Fifty-one percent said they felt the city had become a safer place in the last three years, 10 percent said it was less safe and 37 percent said it was about the same.

According to official police statistics for 1996, New York was safer than it has been in years and there were fewer than 1,000 murders during the calendar year for the first time in almost three decades.
Republican Mayor Rudolph Giuliani was elected in 1993 on a crime-fighting platform and has earned much of the credit for the record decline in serious crimes such as murder, robbery and assault.

When asked specifically whether they thought crime was a problem, 81 percent said it was "a big problem," 17 percent called it a "small problem" and 1 percent said it was "not a problem at all," the poll found.
